soil-env-334.title: Scorecards that rate a field's soil health
soil-env-334.text: You can judge a soil without a laboratory, using a shovel and some patience. A scorecard rates {{ref:soil-env-174}} on scales, drawing on what you see in the soil and in the crop growing on it. In the field, check earthworms, erosion, ease of tillage, structure and color, compaction, water infiltration and drainage. Then rate the crop's appearance, growth rate, root health, drought resistance and yield. Farmers are advised to fill out a scorecard for each major field or soil type every few years, or to send soil to a laboratory that offers soil health analyses.

soil-env-343.title: Push-pull: repelling pests while trapping them
soil-env-343.text: Some pest control works by giving insects somewhere else to go. A perimeter trap crop intercepts a pest before it reaches the main crop. Blue Hubbard squash around summer squash, for example, intercepts striped cucumber beetles. East African push-pull goes further, building on {{ref:soil-agri-217}}. Desmodium, a legume, grows within the corn rows and repels stem borers: that is the push. Grasses planted around the edge attract adult moths: that is the pull. The legume also supplies nitrogen and suppresses weeds.

soil-env-348.title: Why surface residue need not mean more disease
soil-env-348.text: Farmers are often told to bury crop residue because it can harbour pathogens. Yet the same advice promotes leaving {{ref:soil-agri-129}} on the surface and tilling less. Both claims hold, because the system differs. With rotations, conservation tillage, cover crops and organic additions, soil biological diversity and beneficial organisms increase. Crop stress falls, and disease pressure falls with it. In traditional systems a single pathogen more easily comes to dominate.

soil-env-347.title: Symphylans: the pest that likes rich soil
soil-env-347.text: Most soil pests thrive in poor, degraded ground. Symphylans do the opposite. These white, centipede-like arthropods feed on root hairs and rootlets and damage many crops. They prefer soils rich in organic matter, because good structure and old root channels let them move easily. In some fields they appear in spotty, circular patches. Biological activity is not thought to be an adequate defense. Potatoes and beans are damaged less, transplanted tomatoes do better than direct seeded ones, and denser squash planting helps maintain yield. Organic amendments should be imported with care so the pest is not introduced by accident.

soil-env-338.title: Does organic food make people healthier?
soil-env-338.text: The belief that organic food is better for you is widespread, but the evidence is thin. Plants take up nutrients almost entirely as inorganic forms, so nutrients from organic sources are not known to affect human health differently than synthetic ones. Some studies find higher antioxidant levels in organic food. Yet organic eaters usually have better diets, lifestyles and incomes, and no study has tied the antioxidants to better health outcomes. Whether better soil management and organic production improve human health is still debated. The studies cannot separate these confounding factors. See {{ref:soil-env-337}} for the wider link.

soil-env-345.title: How plants arm themselves against disease
soil-env-345.text: A plant attacked in one leaf can raise its defenses in all of them. Plants form hormones and defence proteins in response to signals from microorganisms, making the whole plant resistant to pathogens even far from the infection site. Systemic acquired resistance follows exposure to a pathogen, or even a non-pathogenic organism, and involves salicylic acid and defense proteins that protect against many pathogens. Induced systemic resistance follows root exposure to plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, and involves the hormones jasmonate and ethylene. The roots meet these bacteria in the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}. Some organic amendments induce resistance, but no reliable, cost-effective indicator yet shows whether a soil or amendment is strengthening plant defense. Defenses come in depth: rhizosphere bacteria that compete with or antagonize pathogens, endophytes inside roots that produce antifungal chemicals, and the plant's own chemicals.

soil-env-346.title: Healthy plants resist pests better
soil-env-346.text: Pests are drawn to weakness. Healthy, thriving plants defend themselves better, while drought, nutrient limits or compaction stress them and make them signal weakness to pests. That makes {{ref:soil-env-174}} the foundation of crop pest management. Developing optimal soil health is the basis of it, and it should underpin integrated pest management programs.

soil-env-342.title: Soil practices that hold pests in check
soil-env-342.text:
Many pest problems can be eased through the soil itself. Rotation reduces disease, insect, nematode and weed pressure. Avoiding excess inorganic nitrogen limits insect damage, and adequate calcium or potassium lowers some crop diseases. Less compaction lowers insect and root-disease damage. Composts low in available nitrogen but with active organic matter reduce root rot and leaf disease severity.

A {{ref:soil-agri-066}} adds more. Cover crops, especially in reduced tillage, keep mycorrhizal spore counts high, and selected ones suppress parasitic fungi and nematodes. Cereal rye residue reduces weed seed germination. Reduced tillage and surface residue also keep weed seeds on the surface, where ground beetles, rodents, ants and crickets eat them. Biologically active soils reduce weed seed numbers.

soil-env-286.title: Active carbon: an early sign of soil health
soil-env-286.text: Most of a soil's carbon changes too slowly to watch. Active carbon is the exception: the most readily usable portion of the total organic carbon, as in {{ref:soil-env-108}}. It contributes greatly to the functioning of the soil food web. It is a newer measure that joins established ones such as microbial biomass and activity, enzymes, soil organic matter, total nitrogen, available nutrients, porosity, aggregate stability and compaction. It is the fraction oxidized by potassium permanganate, measured with an inexpensive spectrophotometer. Because it responds quickly to management, it is an early indicator of gains in soil health, as in {{ref:soil-env-177}}.

soil-env-251.title: Locking contaminants in place with binders
soil-env-251.text: Sometimes the cleanest answer is to stop contaminants from moving. Solidification and stabilization mix a binder into contaminated soil to stop or reduce the mobility of contaminants. Stabilization adds reagents that make constituents chemically more stable. Solidification locks contaminants in a solid product that air and rain cannot reach. Binding agents such as cement or asphalt prevent or slow release from the soil. As a form of {{ref:soil-env-012}} for {{ref:soil-env-001}}, its uptake is held back by cheap landfill disposal, doubts about durability and contaminant release, and liability for contaminants left on site. CO2 emissions from the cement used are a growing obstacle.

soil-env-315.title: Organic and inorganic soil contaminants
soil-env-315.text: Soil contaminants fall into two families. Organic contaminants include pesticides, solvents and industrial products. Inorganic ones include metals, salts, nutrients and radionuclides. At Canadian contaminated sites the most common organic contaminants are petroleum hydrocarbons: crude oil, fuels and lubricating oils. Dioxins, furans and PAHs are also organic. Inorganics include heavy and trace metals, metalloids, acids and bases, excess nutrients and salts, and radionuclides, from mine wastes, firing ranges, fly ash and battery disposal. Some help soil ecosystems at background levels. Copper, molybdenum, cobalt and zinc are plant micronutrients but contaminants at high concentrations. Chloride from de-icing or spills can build up and raise electrical conductivity. Excess nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur from misplaced livestock waste can also be contaminants.

soil-env-316.title: Matching the cleanup method to the contaminant
soil-env-316.text: No single cleanup suits every site. The choice depends on the contaminant, the site and the soil properties. Petroleum hydrocarbons differ in molecular weight, solubility, volatility and density. Larger compounds are less volatile and less soluble, and gasoline is lighter and more volatile than lubricating oil. Large insoluble hydrocarbons sorb strongly to soil organic matter and are hard to degrade or remove, especially in fine-textured soils, where aggregates trap them and air and water move poorly. Metals are spread among soil components depending on texture, mineralogy, pH, exchange capacity, organic matter and aeration, so remediation must consider each chemical form. Treatments are biological, chemical or physical, often combined. They are applied ex situ, meaning excavated and treated on or off site, or in situ, meaning treated in place.

soil-env-318.title: Vitrification: melting soil into glass
soil-env-318.text: At 1400 to 2000 °C, soil stops being soil. Vitrification heats it until its silica melts into stable glass and crystalline solids. The heat may come from electrodes and electrical resistance, or from plasma arc technology. Organic contaminants are volatilized, trapped and treated or destroyed. Inorganic contaminants, including radionuclides, are encased. Ex situ incineration is milder, heating soil to 870 to 1370 °C to destroy organic contaminants.

soil-env-317.title: Soil washing and flushing
soil-env-317.text: Contaminants tend to cling to the smallest particles. Soil washing, an ex situ treatment, may separate the silt and clay fines from the coarse material. Because the contaminants cling to the fines, removing them reduces the total mass and volume that needs treatment. In situ soil flushing works differently. It treats the contaminated zone with a solution of water, acid, base, chelating agent, co-solvent or surfactant. It then brings the mobilized contaminants to the surface for disposal, treatment or recirculation.
